standard.title: Compare the target language and English
standard.description: compare target language structures and features with English, using familiar metalanguage
standard.prior_knowledge: Students are developing knowledge of target language grammatical structures and writing systems (AC9LS8EU02) and can recognise some features of the target language sound system (AC9LS8EU01). They have not yet systematically compared the target language with English using metalanguage, though they bring implicit awareness of English grammar from prior schooling.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students compare key structures and features of the target language with English — including grammar, word order, punctuation and register conventions — using familiar metalanguage to describe and discuss language patterns.

nodes.label: Building and using metalanguage
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use a working set of grammatical metalanguage terms to describe and discuss structures in both the target language and English.
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least five metalanguage terms (e.g. noun, verb, adjective, tense, agreement) correctly in describing a language feature in the target language or English.
nodes.typical_width: Build and apply metalanguage across grammatical categories (word classes, tense, agreement, sentence types); use metalanguage to describe and discuss language comparisons; develop a personal or class glossary of metalanguage in both languages.
wider: Research and compare metalanguage in the target language — identify where grammatical terms in the target language reflect its structure differently from English grammatical terms
Use metalanguage to annotate a target language text — label grammatical features and compare the pattern to an equivalent English text
nodes.hinge_reason: Without shared metalanguage, comparison is impressionistic — students can say 'it's different' but not explain how or why. The descriptor's demand to 'compare using metalanguage' requires this vocabulary to be established before substantive comparison is possible.

response_modes.reason: Metalanguage is built through repeated use in meaningful contexts — defining terms once is insufficient. Students need to encounter and use metalanguage across multiple comparison tasks before it becomes functional vocabulary.

success_criteria: Can use at least five metalanguage terms correctly in a discussion of a language feature
Can apply metalanguage to describe a grammatical pattern in the target language

nodes.label: Comparing grammatical structures
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and explain key grammatical differences between the target language and English using metalanguage.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify and explain at least two grammatical differences between the target language and English (e.g. word order, agreement systems, verb forms).
nodes.typical_width: Compare grammatical structures systematically across the target language and English — including word order, agreement systems, verb forms, pronouns and interrogative constructions; explain why the same meaning requires different structures in each language.
wider: Investigate a grammatical feature present in the target language but absent in English (e.g. grammatical gender, formal/informal address distinctions, aspect) — explain what expressive or social function it serves
Compare word order and syntax across a short text in the target language and its English equivalent — map structural differences and discuss their effect on meaning

response_modes.reason: Grammatical comparison requires students to hold two systems in mind simultaneously and reason about structural differences. Explicit comparison frames — 'in English X, in the target language Y, because...' — scaffold the reasoning process before students can conduct comparisons independently.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Investigating grammatical features that exist in the target language but not in English (address forms, gender systems, aspect) is a natural bridge between language structure and intercultural understanding — students encounter how different languages encode different social and conceptual distinctions.
success_criteria: Can identify and explain at least two grammatical differences between the target language and English using metalanguage
Can explain why the same meaning requires different structures in the target language and English for at least one comparison

nodes.label: Comparing register and contextual language use
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify how register shifts in the target language and compare register conventions with English, using examples from familiar contexts.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one example of register distinction in the target language (e.g. formal vs informal address) and compare it with English conventions.
nodes.typical_width: Compare register conventions in the target language and English across familiar contexts (address forms, greeting conventions, digital communication, formal speech); identify language features that shift with register; discuss the social functions of register in each language.
wider: Compare how digital communication conventions (abbreviations, emoticons, informal syntax) differ across the target language and English — identify what is shared and what is language-specific
Investigate the influence of the target language on English or English on the target language — identify loan words and discuss what they reveal about cultural contact

response_modes.reason: Register is contextually defined — students who have only encountered one register context (e.g. classroom formal address) will not generalise. Exposure across digital, social, academic and formal contexts builds the register sensitivity that the descriptor requires.

success_criteria: Can identify at least one register distinction in the target language and compare it with English conventions
Can explain the social function of a specific register choice in the target language with reference to context
